History & Physical (Detailed)

Consult Summary:
38-year-old woman with 3-day history of profuse watery→loose diarrhoea, repeated vomiting, subjective fever, and periumbilical pain after household exposure—clinically suspected infectious gastroenteritis; stool culture and hydration review arranged.

History:
• Presenting complaint: “Serious” diarrhoea and vomiting for 3 days.  
• Course/timeline: Sudden onset; still ongoing, not improving.  
  – Day 3 (today): ≥4 loose BMs; lost overall count.  
  – Last emesis ~2 h before call.  
• Stool: Initially watery, now very loose; no blood or mucus.  
• Vomiting: Empties stomach contents including water, tea, ORS; unable to retain oral intake.  
• Fever: Feels “literally boiling”; no measured temperature.  
• Abdominal pain: Periumbilical, tender to touch, colicky, precedes urge to defecate.  
• Urination: Passing urine; last void 1 h ago; colour not observed; no haematuria.  
• Associated symptoms: No rash.  
• Exposures: Brother with identical illness; school outbreak noted; no recent travel.  
• Self-care tried: Oral rehydration solution (salt-sugar mix) 3×/day for 2 days—ineffective.  
• Review of systems: No prior similar episodes; bowels normally once daily; no constipation; normal menses (LMP 2 w ago).

Past Medical History:
• Generally healthy.  
• Dysmenorrhoea (occasional).  
• No prior GI disorders or abdominal surgery reported.

Medications:
• Vitamin D (dose/route/frequency not documented).  
• Ibuprofen PRN for menstrual cramps (dose/route/frequency not documented).  
• Oral rehydration solution 3×/day (self-initiated).  
Allergies: Not recorded.

Social History:
• Occupation: Graphic designer; working from home today due to illness.  
• Lives with mother and brother.  
• Tobacco: Non-smoker.  
• Alcohol: Occasional pint.  
• Recreational drugs: Denies use.  
• Sexual activity: Not currently sexually active; no contraception.

Family History:
• Brother acutely unwell with similar gastrointestinal symptoms; no other FHx noted.

Physical Examination:
Vitals: Not recorded (remote consultation).  
General: Appears subjectively febrile per patient report.  
Abdomen: Patient reports marked periumbilical tenderness; no further exam possible remotely.  
Other systems: Not examined.

Investigations:
• Planned: Stool sample for culture/analysis.  
• Planned: In-clinic assessment of hydration status (vital signs, possibly labs) at urgent appointment.

Assessment & Plan:
Overall Impression:
Likely infectious gastroenteritis—viral most probable given household cluster, but bacterial cause considered as symptoms persist beyond 72 h with subjective fever.

DDx Integration (brief):
1. Acute viral gastroenteritis (e.g., norovirus) – supports: sudden onset, family cluster, watery diarrhoea & vomiting; opposes: persistence >48 h.  
2. Acute bacterial gastroenteritis – supports: fever, abdominal pain, >3 days duration; opposes: no blood, household spread less typical.  
(Other DDx such as food-borne toxin illness, IBD considered low likelihood; see DDx list—no direct contradictions.)

Issue 1: Possible infectious gastroenteritis
• Arrange urgent clinic visit today/tomorrow for:
  – Stool sample collection for culture ± PCR.  
  – Vital signs and clinical dehydration assessment (postural BP, capillary refill, mucous membranes).  
• Hydration:
  – Continue ORS; take very small, frequent sips.  
  – Monitor urine output; aim for ≥4 voids/day; seek help if markedly reduced or dark.  
• Diet:
  – Bland foods only (toast, biscuits); avoid fruit, vegetables, dairy until settled.  
• Escalation:
  – Go to A&E if unable to keep fluids down, worsening abdominal pain, confusion, dizziness, or blood in stool.  
• Follow-up:
  – Telephone review after stool results or sooner if deterioration.

Issue 2: Pain management
• Simple analgesia if required—paracetamol preferred; avoid NSAIDs if vomiting continues.

Issue 3: Occupational / infection control
• Advise patient to remain off work at least 48 h after last episode of diarrhoea/vomiting to reduce transmission; strict hand hygiene at home.

General plan items:
• Provide clinic contact details and support line for booking urgent appointment.  
• Educate on signs of dehydration and when to seek urgent care.

Quality checks:
● Missing elements: No documented allergies; no objective vitals; limited physical exam—will obtain at clinic visit.  
● Conflicts: None noted between transcript and DDx.  
● Transcript quality: Clear; occasional brief inaudible pauses but key clinical data obtained.
